prompt:
Write an essay of about 800 words on the subject below.

Write it the way an excellent, idiosyncratic human essayist would: someone with real expertise and strong opinions, writing in the first person for their own blog. Commit to a specific thesis that a thoughtful reader might disagree with. Use concrete particulars (names, numbers, incidents, things only someone who had done the work would know) in place of general statements. Vary sentence length. No headings, no bullet points, no summary paragraph at the end, and none of the stock phrases of AI writing.

Output only the essay, with no title.

Subject: a personal essay about moving to a new city
raw:
The standard advice for moving to a new city is to say yes to everything. Go to the coworker's birthday drinks, the Meetup for people who like board games, the free concert in the park, the gallery opening where the wine comes in plastic cups. Explore. Get lost on purpose. Try a new restaurant every week. I followed this advice for the first four months after I moved from Columbus to Philadelphia in the fall of 2021, and it made me lonelier than I have ever been in my life.

The problem with saying yes to everything is that you end up meeting everyone exactly once. I can still list some of them. A man named Derek who restored pinball machines and talked about solenoids for forty minutes. Two sisters from a climbing gym in Kensington who invited me back and whom I never saw again because the next Thursday I went to a trivia night instead. A woman at a rooftop party in Northern Liberties who said "we should get coffee" with the specific warmth of someone who would never get coffee. By December I had something like sixty phone contacts I'd added since August, and I could have called maybe two of them without explaining who I was.

What I had built, it turned out, was a sampler. I knew a little about a lot of neighborhoods. I could tell you which cheesesteak places tourists went to and which ones the guy at my bodega went to. But nobody in the city knew me, and a city where nobody knows you is a hotel with bad room service.

The thing that actually worked was boring, and I stumbled into it because I got sick of trying. In January I stopped exploring. I picked one coffee shop, four blocks from my apartment, a narrow place with a chalkboard menu and a barista named Tomás who had a tattoo of a stingray on his forearm. I went every weekday at 7:40. I ordered the same thing, a cortado, which cost $3.75 and then $4.25 after they raised prices in March. I picked one bar, a dim place on Frankford Avenue that played Steely Dan more often than any bar should, and went every Wednesday. I bought my groceries at the same Acme even though the one in the other direction was nicer. I walked the same route to the El.

Repetition, I've come to believe, is the only real mechanism by which a city takes you in. Novelty feels like progress because every outing has a story attached to it, but stories are not relationships. A relationship in a city is made of a stranger seeing your face on enough separate occasions that you stop being a stranger. Sociologists have a phrase for this, "familiar strangers," from a 1972 paper by Stanley Milgram, who noticed commuters at a train platform recognizing each other for years without speaking. What he didn't emphasize, and what I learned at the coffee shop, is that familiar strangers are a staging area. Somewhere around the fifth week Tomás started my cortado when I walked in. Around the ninth week he asked what I did. Around the fourteenth he told me his band was playing at a basement venue in West Philly, and I went, and I met his roommate, who is now one of my closest friends, and who taught me to make pierogi the way his grandmother in Port Richmond made them, with farmer's cheese and too much butter.

The Wednesday bar took longer. The bartender, a woman in her fifties named Bev, did not care about me at all for two months. Then one night a regular, an old guy named Sal who'd worked at the Navy Yard, was arguing that the Phillies should never have let Jim Thome go, and I said something mildly informed about Thome's 2003 season, and Sal turned and looked at me like I had just been born. After that I had a stool. Not officially. But if I came in and someone was sitting there, Bev would sometimes say, "That's his," and the someone would move.

I know the objection. This sounds narrow, even timid. You moved to a city of a million and a half people to sit on the same stool every Wednesday? Isn't the point of a city that it offers more than you could ever take? But the abundance of a city is exactly what makes it hostile to newcomers. There is always another event, another neighborhood, another person, and so nothing obliges you to come back, and nothing obliges anyone to come back to you. A small town forces repetition on you. A city lets you avoid it forever, and I think a lot of people who stay lonely in big cities for years are people who never stopped sampling.

I still explore, a little. I went to the Wissahickon for the first time last spring, embarrassingly late, and it was beautiful. But I went with the pierogi roommate, and afterward we went to the Wednesday bar even though it was a Saturday, and Bev looked up and said, "Wrong day," and poured my beer before I asked.
